title: Test through the public API
summary: A test that pokes private helpers, fields, and a unit's own collaborator breaks on a pure refactor; a test that only drives the public operation and checks observable results survives it.
signals: tests importing or reflecting into private/internal members (`_method`, reflection, `@VisibleForTesting`)
assertions on an object's private field instead of a returned value or a stored/sent side effect
a test replacing a class's own internally-constructed collaborator instead of one passed to its constructor
a rename or inline refactor that breaks tests without changing any caller-visible behaviour

roles.PreRefactorService: the unit under test, before a behaviour-preserving refactor
roles.PostRefactorService: the same unit under test, after the refactor - identical public behaviour
roles.cancel(): the public operation callers actually invoke
roles.calculateFee() / feeRate: a private helper and field the before test reaches into directly
roles.NotificationFormatter: the unit's own internal collaborator, constructed by it and not injected
roles.OrderRepository (fake): boundary the after tests double: observable state through a real, in-memory implementation
roles.Notifier (spy): boundary the after tests double: an observable call recorded for a state assertion

stages.title: Before
stages.idea: Tests reach past cancel() into a private helper, a private field, and the service's own internal collaborator. Both a pre-refactor and a behaviour-preserving post-refactor implementation ship here, and a passing test proves the same internal-poking assertions no longer hold once the refactor lands.

stages.title: After
stages.idea: The same two implementations are driven only through cancel() and checked by observable results - the identical test case passes against both, because the refactor never touched the contract it exercises.

checks: Why do the before tests pass against the pre-refactor implementation but not the post-refactor one, even though a caller can't tell the two apart?
What makes NotificationFormatter 'a collaborator the unit doesn't own' from the test's point of view, and why does replacing it directly violate 'don't mock what you don't own'?
What would have to be true about a private helper for testing it directly to be the right call instead of a smell?
Why can the exact same test function run unmodified against both PreRefactorService and PostRefactorService in the after stage?
